title: SYSK Selects: How the Panama Canal Works
summary: SYSK Selects episode (originally aired as a full episode) on how the Panama Canal works. The hosts trace the idea of a cross-isthmus route from Balboa's sighting of the Pacific through the failed French sea-level effort led by Ferdinand de Lesseps (about 20,000 deaths, yellow fever and malaria), the U.S. takeover in 1902 after Panama's independence from Colombia, the lock-and-lake design proposed by John Frank Stevens, sanitation work by William Gorgas against mosquito-borne disease, construction under George Washington Goethals, how locks and water use work, the 1977 Carter treaty returning the canal to Panama in 1999, tolls, and the expansion with a third lane approved in 2006. The episode closes with a listener mail correcting an earlier episode on oil reserve audits.
topics: yellow fever and malaria during canal construction

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Selects episode on the Panama Canal, joking about the song 'Panama' and a previous episode.

segments.title: Balboa and the idea of a cross-isthmus route
segments.summary: Balboa sees both oceans from the Darien peak and the idea of a passage forms. The hosts discuss why a shortcut mattered for Spanish trade and for the US trip from New York to San Francisco.

segments.title: Early attempts and the French sea-level canal
segments.summary: Earlier failed outposts are mentioned. The French began a sea-level canal in the 1820s, inspired by steam technology, and the project cost about 20,000 lives. Railroad and the Chagres River come up.

segments.title: Ferdinand de Lesseps and the company's collapse
segments.summary: Ferdinand de Lesseps, who built the Suez Canal, led the French company. Disease, accidents and money losses ended the effort. An attempt to switch to locks with Gustave Eiffel came too late. About eleven miles were dug.

segments.title: US takeover and the 1902 treaty
segments.summary: The US bought the French assets for about forty million dollars and paid Panama ten million. The US backed Panamanian independence from Colombia, and a treaty gave the US a Canal Zone treated as American soil.

segments.title: Lock design, Chagres River and Gatun Lake
segments.summary: Theodore Roosevelt chose chief engineer John Frank Stevens, who favored locks. Stevens proposed damming the Chagres River to create Gatun Lake to carry ships over the mountains.

segments.title: Yellow fever, mosquitoes and sanitation
segments.summary: Ronald Ross's findings on mosquito transmission led to a sanitation campaign under William Gorgas that greatly reduced yellow fever, making construction safer. Many workers who died were Black laborers, and landslides and drownings remained dangers.

segments.title: Construction under Goethals and the three divisions
segments.summary: George Washington Goethals, a lock expert, took over and divided the work into Atlantic, Central and Pacific divisions. Steam shovels and dynamite moved about 96 million cubic yards of earth and rock. The canal opened in 1914.

segments.title: How a transit works and water use
segments.summary: The hosts walk through a transit from the Atlantic side: Gatun locks, Gatun Lake, Gaillard Cut, Pedro Miguel and Miraflores locks, and the Pacific. Each transit takes about eight to ten hours and uses about 52 million gallons of fresh water.

segments.title: Carter treaty, handover and expansion
segments.summary: Jimmy Carter negotiated the return of the canal to Panama, which took effect at the end of 1999. Panama faced traffic and aging-infrastructure issues. A third lane was approved in 2006 to address growth and competition from Nicaragua.

segments.title: Tolls, costs and trivia
segments.summary: Tolls are charged by cargo ton, and the hosts discuss a proposal to base tolls on cargo value. They mention the record toll and Richard Halliburton's cheap swim across the canal. They also note facts about the locks, the Atlantic entrance and the dynamite used.

segments.title: Listener mail on oil reserve audits
segments.summary: A listener named Henry corrects an earlier listener mail about oil reserve audits, explaining that the SEC does not audit companies directly and that audit firms do the work under PCAOB guidelines. The hosts also briefly discuss the Midnight Meat Train.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to the website and social media for more on the Panama Canal and other topics.
